shipped_rows.title_o: Automatization in second language acquisition: What does the coefficient of variation tell us?
shipped_rows.outcome_quote: the CV in the sentence-level tasks decreased as participants’ proficiency level increased.

shipped_rows.title_o: Skilled performance, practice, and the differentiation of speed-up from automatization effects: Evidence from second language word recognition
shipped_rows.outcome_quote: The results of the current study supported Segalowitz and Segalowitz’ (1993) hypothesis (CV decreased as speakers developed automatic processing skills), regardless of whether the data were cleaned (see Table 4). Data cleaning did not affect overall patterns of RTs, standard deviations, and CVs in any task, yet it boosted accuracy rates and caused some contrasts that had initially been nonsignificant to become significant, notably in the semantic classification and sentence verification tasks. Thus, only after data cleaning were the intermediate learners found to retrieve word meanings with more difficulty than the native speakers (p = .009 for RTs, p = .011 for standard deviations, p = .046 for CVs). No such difference was found for the advanced learners versus the native speakers. Similarly, after data cleaning, but not before, nonnative speakers appeared to be less efficient at sentence verification than native speakers, at least when both plausible and implausible sentences were considered together. Finally, the findings of the sentence construction task seemed to be the most robust, given that CV decreased with increasing proficiency level both before and after data cleaning.

corrected_value.title: Automatization in second language acquisition: What does the coefﬁcient of variation tell us?
corrected_value.authors: Hulstijn, J. H., Van Gelderen, A., & Schoonen, R.

prior_scientific_decisions.quote: This study investigates the automatization of sentence processing using the coefﬁcient of variation (CV), a measure of intraindividual processing stability (Segalowitz & Segalowitz, 1993). A smaller CV (i.e., standard deviation to reaction time [RT] ratio) and a positive CV-RT correlation are taken to index increased automatization. Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009) were the ﬁrst to try to validate the use of CV at the sentence level; however, they did not ﬁnd any evidence for automatization in their CV analyses.
prior_scientific_decisions.reason: Wrong original / duplicate of row 67: Segalowitz and Segalowitz (1993) is cited as the theoretical and methodological source that proposed the coefficient of variation (CV) measure in L2 word recognition, not as a finding re-tested by this study. The paper explicitly states that it is a partial conceptual replication of Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009) (doi:10.1017/S0142716409990014), which is already represented in row 67.

prior_scientific_decisions.quote: The general ﬁnding was that RTs, standard deviations, and CVs all decreased as a function of participants’ English proﬁciency level: from intermediate ESL learners (L1 Korean), to advanced ESL learners, to native English speakers. This ﬁnding was in stark contrast to Hulstijn et al.’s (2009) study, who failed to ﬁnd a decrease in Dutch high school students’ CV over three consecutive grade years, in which the students received ESL instruction in school and plentiful exposure to English (e.g., through the media) outside the classroom.
prior_scientific_decisions.reason: Once the wrong original on row 2418 (Segalowitz & Segalowitz, 1993) is corrected to the actual replicated original study, Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009) (making row 2418 a duplicate of row 67), the replication outcome is 'failed' because the observed decrease in CV with proficiency directly contradicts Hulstijn et al.'s (2009) null finding. Agreement with Segalowitz and Segalowitz's (1993) theoretical hypothesis does not make the replication of Hulstijn et al. (2009) successful.
